newsitem.title: USA: New AIDS drug offers hope to resistant patients.
newsitem.headline: New AIDS drug offers hope to resistant patients.

text.p: A new AIDS drug awaiting approval by the Food and Drug Administration offers hope to patients who have failed to respond to other therapies, according to data disclosed Thursday.

San Diego-based Agouron Pharmaceuticals Inc said its protease inhibitor, Viracept, produced a response in 61 percent of patients tested who had developed a resistance to other similar drugs on the market.

Agouron's president, Peter Johnson, said he was optimistic the FDA would approve Viracept sometime during the first half of 1997. The company is also the first AIDS drug maker to develop a powder formulation for children who have difficulty swallowing pills.

Protease inhibitors, a key ingredient in aggressive AIDS drug regimens, work by blocking the virus from leaving a patient's DNA and invading the rest of the body. These drugs, used as part of a three-drug combination, have dramatically improved the health of many AIDS patients, in some cases driving down the viral load to nondetectable levels.
But the drug combination has not been universally successful, since the HIV virus frequently mutates into strains that are resistant to some drugs.

A particularly strong cross resistance has been shown between the protease inhibitors made by Merck and Co Inc and Abbott Laboratories Inc. The other protease inhibitor on the market is made by Hoffman-La Roche .
Agouron's trials also showed the AIDS virus could mutate to resist Viracept. But the means by which it did so was different than with the other drugs.
"The big issue regarding resistance is that there have been some patients who become resistant to one drug, only to find they couldn't find another one they respond to," said Agouron's Johnson.
"What we have seen so far with Viracept is a different situation. When we have gone back to patients who have become resistant to other drugs, we found they generally remained sensitive to Viracept."
Agouron said it tested 23 patients who were resistant to other protease inhibitors and 14 of them were sensitive to Viracept.
